implementation_notes: Rust inverts the classic arrangement: Mutex<T> owns the protected data and the only route to it is the MutexGuard returned by lock(), so a method that forgets to lock cannot even see the field - the discipline other languages enforce by convention, the compiler enforces here. Condvar is the monitor condition; wait consumes and returns the guard so the state cannot be touched without re-acquiring, and wait_while packages the predicate loop. Poisoning turns a panic inside the critical section into a visible error for later lockers, and Arc<Mutex<T>> is how the object is shared between threads. Blocking primitives are the default; async code replaces them with tokio::sync::Mutex.
pitfalls: Poisoning makes every lock() a Result: unwrapping re-panics after any panic inside the critical section, and ignoring PoisonError hides the original failure.
MutexGuard is not Send, so a std guard must not be held across an await; the compiler often rejects it, but not always, and holding it blocks a runtime worker.
Condvar::wait re-acquires the same mutex and panics if different mutexes are used over its lifetime; spurious wakeups still require a predicate loop (or wait_while).

variants.name: tokio::sync::Mutex (async, guard held across await)
variants.implementation_notes: For async services the blocking std primitives would stall a runtime worker, so the monitor lock becomes tokio::sync::Mutex: lock is async and yields instead of blocking, the guard may be held across await points, and acquisition is FIFO. There is no condition variable - waiting for a predicate means dropping the guard and awaiting a Notify, a watch or a channel, or re-checking after each await in a loop. Tokio's own documentation still recommends the std Mutex when the guard is not held across an await, and message passing to a spawned owning task when the object guards an I/O resource, so the async mutex is the targeted choice rather than the default.
pitfalls: Holding the async guard across a long await serialises the object for the whole suspension; keep the critical section short and drop the guard before waiting.
tokio's Mutex does not poison on panic, so a panicking task can leave the guarded data inconsistent - validate on re-entry or encode the invariant in types.
Mixing std locks with tokio locks in inconsistent order, or awaiting while holding a std guard, is a deadlock risk that the compiler does not always catch.
